sections.title: Sheḥita
sections.html:
The Torah permitted Israel to eat the meat of domestic animals (behema), wild animals (ḥaya) and birds, on condition that they are slaughtered according to halakha, as it is stated (Devarim 12:21): "You shall slaughter of your herd and of your flock which the Lord has given you, as I have commanded you" (Ḥullin 28a). And anyone who eats meat that was not made permissible through sheḥita (ritual slaughter) transgresses a Torah prohibition of 'ever min ha-ḥai' (a limb from a living animal) or 'nevela' (carcass).

Ever min ha-ḥai: A limb or meat from a domestic animal, wild animal or bird that was cut from them while they were still alive is forbidden to eat by Torah law. And even if the animals from which they were taken are afterwards slaughtered, it is forbidden to eat them. This prohibition applies also to the descendants of Noaḥ, as it is stated (Bereshit 9:4): "But flesh with its life, which is its blood, you shall not eat" (Sanhedrin 57a). And it is likewise stated to Israel (Devarim 12:23): "And you shall not eat the life with the flesh" (Ḥullin 102b).

Nevela: If the animal died of disease, of old age, in an accident, or from sheḥita not performed according to halakha, it is a nevela and forbidden to eat, as it is stated (Devarim 14:21): "You shall not eat anything that dies of itself (nevela); you may give it to the stranger who is within your gates, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner, for you are a holy people to the Lord your God."

Tereifa: If the animal was slaughtered according to halakha but had a defect that would cause its death within a year, it is a tereifa and forbidden to eat, as it is stated (Shemot 22:30): "And you shall be holy men to Me, and you shall not eat flesh torn (tereifa) in the field; you shall cast it to the dogs." With regard to the prohibition of eating, nevela, tereifa and ever min ha-ḥai are equal, for anyone who eats a kezayit of meat from any of them deliberately, and there were witnesses who warned him, is liable to lashes. However, with regard to the laws of ritual impurity there is a difference between them: a nevela is impure, whereas a tereifa is not impure. Today the laws of impurity and purity are not in practice, since we have no way of becoming purified from the impurity of a corpse.

All the mitzvot connected to sheḥita pertain to domestic animals, wild animals and birds, but kosher fish and locusts do not require sheḥita, and consequently the prohibitions of nevela, tereifa and ever min ha-ḥai do not apply to them (Ḥullin 27b; above 17:7-8).

After the sheḥita, as long as the animal is still convulsing, it is forbidden to eat its meat, because only after all its life has left it is it fit to be eaten, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:26): "You shall not eat with the blood," and one of the prohibitions we learned from this verse is that you shall not eat of the meat while vitality still remains in the animal (Sanhedrin 63a; SA YD 27:1). If the slaughtered creature is a wild animal or a bird, there is a mitzva to cover its blood (below, section 9).

Even after the sheḥita has been carried out according to halakha, one must still be careful about several prohibitions, and they are: the prohibition of eating blood, the prohibition of eating the gid ha-nasheh (sciatic nerve), and the prohibition of eating ḥelev (forbidden fat) of a domestic animal.

As we have already learned (in chapter 14), the matter of eating the meat of animals is morally complex, for originally man was not permitted to kill animals in order to eat their meat; but after the sin of Adam and the Flood, the world descended from its level and man was permitted to eat animals. Sheḥita is a special mitzva that the Holy One, blessed be He, gave to Israel in order to elevate the animal's meat from its level so that it becomes fit for the stature of holy Israel. And so it is stated: "You shall not eat anything that dies of itself … for you are a holy people to the Lord your God" (Devarim 14:21); "And you shall be holy men to Me … you shall not eat tereifa" (Shemot 22:30).

sections.title: The Laws of Sheḥita
sections.html:
The laws of sheḥita were given to Moshe at Sinai, as it is stated (Devarim 12:21): "You shall slaughter of your herd and of your flock which the Lord has given you, as I have commanded you" (Ḥullin 28a). In sheḥita one must cut the two simanim (signs), which are the trachea (kaneh) and the esophagus (veshet). The simanim are the sources of life: the trachea is the source of oxygen, and the esophagus is the source of food, and by cutting them the source of the animal's vitality is severed (SA YD 21:1). In order to prevent tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim (the suffering of animals), and because of the prohibition of eating blood, one must cut together with the simanim the arteries and veins as well, because once the arteries are cut the animal no longer feels pain and its life departs without suffering, and by cutting them the blood, which is forbidden to eat, comes out (below, section 3).1

The sheḥita is performed with a sharp knife from the front of the neck toward the nape, that is, on the soft side of the neck where the simanim and the arteries are located. But if one slaughtered from the direction of the nape, since he immediately struck the vertebral bone and cut it, the animal becomes a nevela, and it will no longer help if he continues cutting until he reaches the two simanim. If he began to slaughter from the sides of the neck, as long as he cut the two simanim without touching the vertebrae, his sheḥita is kosher. In turkeys and pigeons the simanim are located at the sides of the neck, and the shoḥet (slaughterer) must hold them toward the neck [?], so that he is certain that he slaughters them without striking the vertebrae (SA YD 20:3-4).

Five laws of sheḥita were given to Moshe at Sinai: shehiya, derasa, ḥalada, hagrama and ikur, and if one violated one of them, the meat becomes a nevela.

Shehiya (pausing): The act of sheḥita must be done continuously, and if one paused even for any amount of time, his sheḥita is invalid. Although the Sages said that the disqualifying pause is the length of time of a sheḥita (Ḥullin 32a), nevertheless, since according to many of the Rishonim it is the time needed to cut most of the simanim, and it is difficult to estimate this measure, which is less than a second, therefore the stringent practice is to disqualify for any pause whatsoever (Rashi, Mahari Weil, Rema 23:2, Kaf Ha-ḥayim 13).

Derasa (pressing): The sheḥita must be done by cutting, by drawing the knife back and forth, and not by pressing the knife into the neck; whenever one pressed the knife into the neck, even slightly, this is derasa and the sheḥita is invalid. If the knife is twice as long as the width of the neck, after the fact (be-di'avad) it is possible to slaughter the animal in one motion, but initially (le-khatḥila) one slaughters with a knife whose length is double the width of the neck and with a forward and backward stroke, in order to avoid any concern of possible derasa (SA YD 24:1-6; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 9; Simla Ḥadasha 3).

Ḥalada (burying): One who inserts the knife into the neck and cuts from there — this is ḥalada and the sheḥita is invalid. Ḥalada means concealing (like a ḥulda, a weasel, that hides in holes), for he inserts and conceals the knife within the neck. If the animal had a great deal of wool on its neck and he inserted the knife beneath the wool and slaughtered, this is a case of possible ḥalada, and the animal's meat is forbidden to eat (Ḥullin 30b; SA YD 24:7-8). If an animal has thick wool on its neck, the practice is to shear it before the sheḥita.

Hagrama (deviating): The place of the cut is in the neck; one who slaughters beyond the boundary of the neck, toward the mouth or toward the lungs and stomach — this is hagrama and his sheḥita is invalid. So that there will be no concern that the sheḥita is disqualified through hagrama, the practice is to slaughter in the middle of the neck (SA YD 20:1-3; 24:12-14).

Ikur (tearing): There are two explanations of this disqualification: 1) One who slaughters with a knife that has a nick — the nick tears the trachea and esophagus, and the sheḥita is invalid. 2) When one of the simanim was dislodged from its place of attachment in the animal's neck and was cut in that state, the sheḥita is invalid (SA YD 24:15-18).

sections.title: Sheḥita and Compassion
sections.html:
Although the mitzva of sheḥita is a Divine mitzva whose full reason we cannot understand, it is clear that the laws of sheḥita contain an expression of compassion. As explained in the comprehensive book of Rabbi Dr. Levinger ('Ha-sheḥita Ve-tza'ar Ba'alei Ḥayim' — Sheḥita and Animal Suffering), sheḥita is the gentlest way of killing an animal without torment. For the artery that supplies most of the blood to the brain passes through the place of the sheḥita, and so immediately after the sheḥita there is no longer any blood supply to the brain. Therefore, at the time when the sensation of pain should reach the cerebral cortex, where the sensation of pain is registered, because of the lack of blood and oxygen the cerebral cortex is unable to register the pain. Even before the main artery is cut, the pain is hardly felt, because the sheḥita must be done with a sharp and smooth knife, in a quick motion, and in this way the sensation of pain is hardly felt. In addition, the practice is to lay the animal down before the sheḥita, and this reduces its suffering, because this position distracts it from the act of sheḥita, and also the cutting off of the supply of blood and oxygen to the brain occurs quickly in this position. In addition, research has found that animals do not sense that they are about to be killed, for even after animals standing next to them were slaughtered, they continued to chew grass calmly, whereas at a time of panic they stop chewing.

It should be noted that the sheḥita of domestic and wild animals is more stringent than the sheḥita of birds, for in domestic and wild animals one must cut two simanim (trachea and esophagus), whereas in birds it suffices after the fact to cut one siman (Ḥullin 27b). It is possible to explain that since the nervous system of birds is less developed and their suffering is lighter, the law of their sheḥita is also more lenient (above 15:1, the second principle). It can likewise be explained that since the nervous system and brain of fish and locusts are much less developed, the Torah did not command that they be slaughtered, and the prohibition of ever min ha-ḥai also does not apply to them (below, section 11; above 17:7-8).

There was an incident with Rabbi Yehuda Ha-nasi (Rabbi), the editor of the Mishna, in which a calf that was being taken to slaughter fled from the shoḥet, hid its head in the corner of Rabbi's garment, and lowed in weeping. And although it appears that animals do not sense that they are about to be killed, it appears that the calf suffered from being dragged by force and hurt, and therefore it fled. Rabbi pushed the calf away and said to it: "Go to the shoḥet, for this is what you were created for." At that moment a great accusation was aroused against Rabbi in Heaven, and they said: since he did not have compassion on that calf, severe sufferings shall come upon him. And so for thirteen years Rabbi suffered from pain in his gums and from pain in passing urine. One day his maidservant was cleaning the house and found small young of a weasel (a rat), and was about to throw them out. Rabbi said to her: "Leave them, for it is written (Tehillim 145:9): 'And His mercies are over all His works.'" At that moment they said in Heaven: since he had compassion on animals, it is fitting to have compassion on him as well, and the sufferings departed from him (Bava Metzia 85a).

And although according to halakha it is permitted to slaughter animals in order to eat their meat, we learn from this story that it is fitting to feel a little sorrow about it. For in truth, in the ideal state of the world, human beings could have sufficed with food from plants. Only after the entire world descended from its stature in the wake of the sin of Adam and the sin of the Flood did the law of nature prevail, and human beings eat animals. In accordance with the great stature and piety of Rabbi Yehuda Ha-nasi, it would have been fitting for him to have a little compassion on the calf, so that it would calm down and agree to go to slaughter. And since he paid no heed to the suffering of the calf, sufferings came upon him (Rav Kook in 'Ḥazon Ha-tzimḥonut Ve-ha-shalom' 1). The Sages said that Rabbi did not reject his sufferings, and asked in his prayer that if it was fitting for him to be refined through sufferings, the sufferings should continue to afflict him. And since these sufferings came upon him according to his moral stature, in order to refine and purify him, the Sages said that during all those years in which he suffered, the rains were not withheld (Bava Metzia, ibid.).

sections.title: The Shoḥet
sections.html:
All Jews are fit to slaughter, men and women, adults and minors, and even a Jew who sometimes stumbles in eating tereifot (Ḥullin 2a; SA YD 1:1; 2:2). But a non-Jew who slaughtered, even if he slaughtered according to halakha, his sheḥita is invalid and the meat is nevela, for only one who was commanded regarding sheḥita is fit to slaughter. Likewise, a Jew who worships idols, or desecrates Shabbat publicly, or eats nevelot out of spite — his sheḥita is invalid (SA YD 2:1-5).

Although all Jews are fit to slaughter, their sheḥita is kosher only if it was done according to halakha. Therefore, if the one who slaughtered is expert in the five laws of sheḥita, we rely on his sheḥita. And if he is not expert, his sheḥita is kosher only if a Jew who is expert in the halakha was present and saw that he slaughtered according to halakha. Initially, even one who has learned the laws should not slaughter by himself until he has become accustomed to slaughtering several times in the presence of an experienced shoḥet, who will see whether he indeed knows how to slaughter and does not faint because of the blood (Rambam, Hilkhot Sheḥita 4:1-3).

Since checking the knife requires skill, the Sages established that every person who wishes to slaughter must first bring his knife to the local rabbi so that he can check whether the knife is fit. Although any Torah scholar can check this, out of respect for the rabbi of the place they brought the knife specifically to him (Ḥullin 17b). Through this check, the rabbi could assess whether there was a need to instruct the owner of the knife to study the laws of sheḥita again. They were especially strict with meat sellers, that they not slaughter without showing the knife to the rabbi. And they would excommunicate a butcher who did not show his knife to the rabbi. And if, in addition to not showing the knife to the rabbi, the knife was also found to be nicked, they would revoke his right to sell meat, and announce that from then on any meat he sold would be considered tereifa (Ḥullin 18a; SA YD 18:17).

In villages where many Jews raised domestic animals and poultry and learned to slaughter them, the responsibility rested on each and every individual, and therefore they could suffice with having everyone who slaughters, whether for himself or for others, show the knife to the rabbi beforehand. However, in cities where they needed professional shoḥetim for all the members of the community, it was necessary to check carefully that they were indeed God-fearing and expert in their craft. For if, Heaven forbid, an unworthy shoḥet is appointed, he may feed the entire community nevelot and tereifot for years.

And so we find in recent generations, after most of Israel began to live in large communities and people became more specialized, each in his own field, that the craft of sheḥita also became a defined role of particular people. Then the great sages of Israel established that a person would not be appointed as a shoḥet without receiving a certificate from an authorized rabbi attesting that he is God-fearing and expert in the laws. In addition they established that the rabbi of the place would be responsible for the kashrut of the meat in his community. For this purpose the rabbis would authorize special rabbis to be responsible on their behalf for the work of sheḥita and the inspection for tereifot, with the checking of the knives being only one detail of their area of responsibility (see Rema 1:1).

Since sheḥita is connected to the holiness of Israel (above, section 1), and the shoḥet must elevate the animal from its animal level so that it becomes fit to add life and strength to Israel for engaging in Torah and mitzvot, it is fitting to choose a shoḥet of good character, righteous and God-fearing. It is likewise fitting that the shoḥet be compassionate and gentle, and that he not butcher the animals with coarseness of heart and cruelty.

sections.title: The Blessing over the Mitzva
sections.html:
The shoḥet first recites: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning sheḥita." If he forgot and did not recite the blessing, he has lost the blessing, and the sheḥita is kosher (SA YD 19:1).

One who is about to slaughter many animals recites one blessing over all of them. He should not speak from the time of the blessing until he has slaughtered all of them, but about matters connected with the sheḥita he is permitted to speak.

Although it is possible that in the inspection after the sheḥita the animal will be found to be a tereifa, and it will turn out that the sheḥita did not serve to permit it for eating, one recites a blessing over the sheḥita of each and every animal, because most animals are kosher. However, if while the animal was still alive a doubt arose about its kashrut, for example, that it was sick or injured, one should not recite a blessing before slaughtering it, since it is doubtful whether the sheḥita will serve to permit it. After the sheḥita they should hasten to inspect it, and if it turns out to be kosher, the shoḥet should recite the blessing immediately (Rema 19:1; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 8; 11). It is better to slaughter an ordinary animal or a bird together with the animal about which a doubt arose, and to recite the blessing over them first, and with his blessing he will also cover the animal about which a doubt arose (Taz and Shakh).

sections.title: The Knife
sections.html:
The sheḥita must be done with a knife. Strictly speaking, it is permitted to slaughter with any detached object, such as flint, glass or wood, provided they are sharp and smooth without a nick (Ḥullin 15b; SA YD 6:1-2). But the practice is to slaughter with a metal knife, because metal is a strong material and suitable for sharpening the knife.

Whenever the knife has a nick, the sheḥita is invalid, because at the place of the nick the knife tears the simanim instead of cutting them. All this is on condition that the nick 'catches', that is, that if a hair were passed over the knife, it would get caught at the place of the nick (Ḥullin 17b; SA YD 18:2). Therefore, before the sheḥita one must check the knife on its three sides. This is how it is done: one carefully passes the fingernail along the right side of the knife's edge along its entire length, back and forth, and likewise afterwards along its left side, and afterwards along the edge of the knife back and forth. If a nick is found, one sharpens the knife again until it is smooth. Originally they would also check the three sides of the knife on the flesh of the finger, but in recent generations, following the development of the metal industry, knives have become sharper and it is difficult to check them on the flesh for fear that the finger will be cut, and therefore the shoḥetim and inspectors suffice with checking on the tip of the fingernail (Ḥullin 17b; SA YD 18:9; Beit David 5).

After the sheḥita one must check the knife again, and if a nick is found in it, the animal is forbidden, because we are concerned that the knife may have been nicked on the animal's hide, and the cutting of the simanim that was done afterwards was done with a nicked knife. To prevent this, one removes the mud and clay from the neck of the animals, and if they have thick wool, one shaves it (SA YD 18:12).

One who slaughters many animals must check the knife between one sheḥita and the next, for if he checks only at the end and finds a nick in the knife, all the animals slaughtered since the last check are forbidden. However, in industrial sheḥita of poultry, they do not check the knife before each sheḥita; rather, they slaughter many birds continuously and afterwards check the knife, and if a nick is found in it, they declare tereifa all the birds slaughtered since the previous check of the knife. This is because the loss caused by delaying the sheḥita through checking the knives is greater than the loss that will be caused when occasionally a nicked knife is found and they must declare many birds tereifa (SA and Rema YD 18:11; see Beit David, Yesodei Ha-halakha 18:6:3 [?]). It should be noted that following the development of the metal industry, knives today are made of high-quality metal, and only rarely is a disqualifying nick found in the knives.

sections.title: A Newborn Calf and a Chick Fit for Sheḥita
sections.html:
When an animal has given birth to young, if we know that it completed its entire period of gestation, it is permitted to slaughter it immediately. But if we do not know whether it completed its period of gestation, which is nine months for a large animal (an ox) and five months for a small animal (sheep and goat), one must wait until the eighth day after its birth, when it is already clear that it is not a nefel (non-viable offspring), and it is permitted to slaughter it. Since in practice we do not know whether the animal completed its entire period of gestation, one does not slaughter the young of an animal before the eighth day after birth (SA YD 15:2). However, with regard to sacrifices, there is a positive Torah commandment not to bring an animal as a sacrifice before it reaches its eighth day, as it is stated (Vayikra 22:27): "When an ox or a sheep or a goat is born, it shall be seven days under its mother, and from the eighth day and onward it shall be accepted as a fire offering to the Lord." But with regard to slaughtering domestic and wild animals for ordinary (non-sacred) eating, one does not slaughter before the eighth day only because one must make sure that the young is not a nefel.

A fully formed chick that has hatched from its egg and come out into the world is fit for sheḥita. But while it is still inside the egg it is considered a winged creeping creature (sheretz ha-of), and therefore if they broke the eggshell and took it out, it is forbidden to slaughter it and eat it. Only after it grows and becomes like other birds will it be fit for sheḥita (SA YD 15:1; Simla Ḥadasha 1). According to many, even a chick that hatched its shell by itself should not be slaughtered as long as it does not yet have large feathers on its wings, because of 'bal teshaktzu' (the prohibition against making oneself repulsive) (Shakh 15:2; Tevu'ot Shor 15:2; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 2-3. The Taz permitted it).

sections.title: Oto Ve-et Beno (An Animal and Its Young)
sections.html:
The Torah forbade slaughtering an animal and its son or daughter on one day, as it is stated (Vayikra 22:28): "And whether it be ox or ewe, you shall not slaughter it and its young both in one day." Even when one first slaughtered the son or daughter, it is forbidden to slaughter the mother on that day. This prohibition applies even to two Jews, so that if one slaughtered an animal, it is forbidden for his fellow to slaughter its son or its mother.

Whenever a young animal follows after its mother, even if it is not remembered with certainty that it was born from her, there is a presumption (ḥazaka) that she is its mother, and it is forbidden to slaughter them on one day. But ordinarily one need not be concerned about slaughtering two animals from one herd lest one be the mother of the other (Tur and SA YD 16:5).

The main prohibition concerns the mother and her young, because generally it is not known who the father is, since there is no connection between the father and the young that issue from his seed, for only the mother nurses her young when they are small. The Tanna'im disagreed about a case in which it is known with certainty who the father of a particular animal is. In practice it was ruled that because of the doubt one must be stringent, and whenever the matter is known with certainty, it is forbidden to slaughter it and its son on one day; but if one transgressed and slaughtered, he is not punished with lashes (Rambam, Hilkhot Sheḥita 12:11; SA YD 16:1).

A 'day' means a full day and night, so that if one slaughtered the mother at the beginning of the night, he should not slaughter the son until the end of the day. If he slaughtered the mother close to sunset, he may slaughter the son at night, for from the time three stars have come out a new day has begun (SA YD 16:4).

One who buys an animal in the market may slaughter it that same day and need not be concerned that its mother or son may also have been slaughtered that day. But if the seller knows that he sold its mother or son in order for them to be slaughtered that same day, he must warn the buyer not to slaughter the animal he bought on that day. The Sages established that on four occasions in the year, even when the buyer did not tell the seller that he intends to slaughter the animal that day, the seller must warn the second buyer, who bought its mother or son, not to slaughter them that day, because presumably the first buyer bought the animal in order to slaughter it that same day. These are the days: the eve of Shemini Atzeret, the eve of Pesaḥ, the eve of Atzeret (Shavu'ot), and the eve of Rosh Ha-shana (Ḥullin 83a; SA YD 16:6). In large communities where it was customary to slaughter many animals on Fridays (Shabbat eves), the rabbis ruled to be stringent about this on every Shabbat eve as well (Zivḥei Tzedek 16:17; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 31).

Today in slaughterhouses the practice is to designate special days for slaughtering calves, special days for slaughtering nursing cows, and special days for slaughtering breeding males, so that it is not possible that a mother and its son will be slaughtered on one day.

If one transgressed and slaughtered a mother and its son on one day, some say that although he violated a Torah prohibition, the meat is permitted to eat (Rambam, Ramban and Rashba), and some say that one should refrain from eating the second one until the end of the day-and-night (Behag, Rosh and Ran; see SA YD 16:3). This prohibition applies only to the sheḥita of a mother and its son, but if the first one died by itself, or its sheḥita was invalid, there is no prohibition against slaughtering the second one on the same day (SA YD 16:9).

This prohibition applies to domestic animals (behemot) and not to wild animals (ḥayot), that is, to domesticated animals and not to wild beasts. It also does not apply to birds.

Some of the Rishonim explained that the reason for the prohibition is to instill in us the trait of compassion, for although we eat the meat of animals, nevertheless it is not fitting to slaughter the mother and its son together (Rambam, Moreh Nevukhim 3:48; Ramban on Devarim 22:6).

sections.title: Kisui Ha-dam (Covering the Blood)
sections.html:
One who slaughters a wild animal or a bird is obligated to cover its blood, as it is stated (Vayikra 17:13): "And any man of the Children of Israel, or of the strangers who dwell among them, who hunts any game, wild animal or bird, that may be eaten, he shall pour out its blood and cover it with dust." But one who slaughters a domestic animal need not cover its blood, as it is stated (Devarim 12:24): "You shall pour it out on the ground like water." What wild animals and birds have in common is that they are accustomed to living in freedom and must be hunted, whereas domestic animals are accustomed to living with people who feed them. Although chickens, which are birds, are also accustomed to living with people, the Torah did not distinguish between the kinds of birds; rather, since most birds are accustomed to living in freedom, the few domesticated species are also included with them (SA YD 28:1; Shakh 1).

The Tanna'im disagreed about the law of the wild ox (shor ha-bar): according to the Sages it is a kind of domestic animal that fled to the wilderness and became a wild ox, and according to Rabbi Yosei it is a kind of wild animal, since it grows up wild (Kilayim 8:6). According to most poskim the halakha follows the Sages that it is a kind of domestic animal and there is no need to cover its blood (Tur and SA YD 28:4). Some are concerned initially for the opinion of those who hold that it is a kind of wild animal, and cover its blood without a blessing (Rema 28:4; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 24).

One who covers the blood first recites: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning covering the blood with dust." One who slaughters many wild animals and birds need not cover the blood of each one separately; rather, when he finishes slaughtering all of them, he recites "concerning covering the blood with dust" and covers the blood of all of them together (SA YD 28:9; 19:5).

The shoḥet must cover the blood, and if he did not cover it and another Jew saw the blood, he is obligated to cover it, for all of Israel are obligated in the mitzva (SA YD 28:8). A wild animal or bird that was slaughtered without its blood being covered, although the mitzva was neglected with regard to them, their meat is kosher to eat (Rema 28:1).

The mitzva of covering the blood applies only to the blood of a wild animal or bird that has been rendered fit for eating; but if the shoḥet erred in his sheḥita and the animal became a nevela, or a defect was found in it and it became a tereifa, there is no need to cover its blood. Therefore, before covering the blood, one checks the knife and the simanim that were cut, and everything that is usually checked for fear of tereifot, and if they are found to be kosher, one recites the blessing and covers the blood (SA YD 28:17-20).

Many explained (Sefer Ha-ḥinukh 187) that this mitzva contains an expression of shame and apology for our not yet having reached the moral level according to which it is not fitting to eat animals, and therefore we cover the blood. We were not commanded to cover the blood of a domestic animal, since its sustenance comes from man, and if the Torah had commanded us to apologize for slaughtering it as well, the moral balance would have been upset (our master Rav Kook in 'Ḥazon Ha-tzimḥonut Ve-ha-shalom' 14).

sections.title: The Manner of Covering
sections.html:
The covering must be with dust, that is, with what is called dust or in which seeds can be sown and will grow. Included in this are earth, sand, dung, ground earthenware, ash of things that were burned, flax tow, and sawdust of carpenters that comes out of wood when it is sawn. One does not cover with wet sand, because anything that does not crumble into small particles is not considered dust. And one does not cover with sulfur and salt, which are not dust (SA YD 28:23-24; Simla Ḥadasha 27-29).

The covering must be below and above. Therefore, one must slaughter a wild animal or bird over loose dust, and if he comes to slaughter in a place where there is already loose dust, he must say aloud that this dust shall be designated for covering, and slaughter over it. The blessing is recited before covering the blood from above (SA YD 28:5; Shakh 12). If he erred and slaughtered over stones, he should drag the blood to a place where there is loose dust, so that it will be covered with dust from below, and afterwards cover the blood from above. And if there is no possibility of dragging the blood to a place where there is loose dust, he should cover the blood in its place, and although he did not fulfill the mitzva properly, he recites the blessing on covering the blood (SA YD 28:7; Simla Ḥadasha 8). One must cover the blood respectfully, by hand or with a utensil and not with the foot, so that the mitzvot will not be degraded in his eyes (SA YD 28:6).

There is no obligation to cover all the blood; rather, one fulfills the obligation by covering part of the blood, provided that he covers part of the dam ha-nefesh (the life-blood), which is the blood that spurts from the neck immediately after the sheḥita. When possible, it is good to cover all the blood.2

In poultry slaughterhouses, the blood flows into a large container, and one must take care to place dust or sawdust in it from the outset so that the blood will flow onto it, and after the end of each sheḥita shift, the shoḥetim cover the blood in the container.

If one slaughtered and the blood was absorbed into the ground, as long as its mark is still discernible, there is a mitzva to cover it (SA YD 28:10). If one covered the blood and the wind came and uncovered it, he is not obligated to cover it again, since he has already fulfilled its mitzva. And if before the shoḥet managed to cover the blood the wind came and covered it with dust, the shoḥet is exempt from covering it, and if the blood became uncovered again, he is obligated to cover it (Mishna Ḥullin 87b; SA YD 28:11); however, according to many Aḥaronim he should cover it without a blessing (Darkhei Teshuva 81).

sections.title: Animals That Do Not Require Sheḥita
sections.html:
Domestic animals, wild animals and birds require sheḥita by Torah law, but fish and locusts do not require sheḥita, and the prohibitions of nevela, tereifa and blood do not apply to them, and in whatever way they died it is permitted to eat them. The prohibition of ever min ha-ḥai also does not apply to them, and therefore there is no prohibition against cutting a limb from them, rinsing it and eating it while they are alive. Some say that one should not eat in this way because it is a trait of cruelty (Da'at Kohen 12). According to all opinions it is forbidden to bite into them while they are alive, because of the prohibition of 'bal teshaktzu', according to which it is forbidden to eat in a repulsive manner (SA and Rema YD 13:1).

Although the mitzva of sheḥita is a ḥok (statute) whose full understanding is beyond our grasp, it is possible to explain that there is no need to slaughter fish and locusts, and the prohibition of ever min ha-ḥai also does not apply to them, because their brain and nervous system are less developed than those of domestic animals, wild animals and birds, and therefore it is reasonable that their sensation of pain and their awareness of life are also dimmer (as explained above in section 3).

When a pregnant animal was slaughtered according to halakha, its sheḥita also permits the fetus in its womb. This fetus is called a 'ben pekua'. It makes no difference whether this fetus was alive or dead; since its mother was slaughtered according to halakha, it too is permitted to eat like its mother. However, the Sages said that if the 'ben pekua' walked on the ground, it requires sheḥita because of mar'it ayin (appearances), for if they do not slaughter it, it will appear as though people are eating a domestic or wild animal without sheḥita. But since according to the strict law it does not require sheḥita, even if it had tereifot, its meat is permitted to eat, for as long as its mother is kosher, it too is kosher (SA YD 13:2). And if its mother was found to be a tereifa, it too is forbidden to eat. And if they waited until it lived eight days and stood on its feet, its law is like that of other domestic and wild animals, which can be permitted through sheḥita (SA YD 13:3; Shakh 11).3
